prompt.context: Midwest Hospital is a research-based hospital that takes pride in its joint replacement surgery department. Recently, Midwest Hospital did a P&L analysis for all departments and found that the joint replacement surgery department is generating losses. The CEO has asked us to help out. The focus of this case is only on the joint replacement surgery department; there are no specific financial targets.
prompt.question: The joint replacement surgery department is unprofitable. What is driving the losses, and what should Midwest Hospital do?

clarifying_info.q: Are there specific financial targets we need to hit?
clarifying_info.a: No, there are no financial targets.

clarifying_info.q: Should we consider other departments beyond joint replacement?
clarifying_info.a: No, focus only on joint replacement surgery.

exhibits.title: Patient Mix
exhibits.shows: Breakdown of joint replacement surgery patients by payer type, showing number of surgeries, list price, and invoiced (actual) price per surgery for each payer category.
exhibits.data: Payer types: Commercial (Enterprises) 100 surgeries, list price $40,000, invoiced price $40,000; Insurance (HMO) 300 surgeries, list price $40,000, invoiced price $20,000; Medicare (Government) 600 surgeries, list price $40,000, invoiced price $15,000. Total surgeries: 1,000.

exhibits.title: Joint Replacement Department P&L
exhibits.shows: Income statement for the joint replacement surgery department showing total revenue, variable costs broken down by category, fixed costs broken down by category, total costs, and profit/loss.
exhibits.data: Revenue: $19M. Variable costs: Physician $5M, Materials $5M, Others $4M (total VC = $14M). Fixed costs: Facilities $3.5M, Others $3.5M (total FC = $7M). Total Costs: $21M. Profit: ($2M).

exhibits.title: Competitive Benchmark
exhibits.shows: Comparison of Midwest Hospital against four competitors across number of surgeries, patient mix (% Commercial, % HMO/Insurance, % Medicare), and whether the hospital is profitable.
exhibits.data: Midwest Hospital: 1,000 surgeries, 10% Commercial, 30% HMO, 60% Medicare, Not profitable. Comp A: 1,200 surgeries, 20% Commercial, 20% HMO, 40% Medicare, Profitable. Comp B: 800 surgeries, 30% Commercial, 20% HMO, 50% Medicare, Profitable. Comp C: 900 surgeries, 10% Commercial, 20% HMO, 70% Medicare, Profitable. Comp D: 1,000 surgeries, 5% Commercial, 25% HMO, 75% Medicare (note: Comp D has fewer commercial patients and heavier Medicare mix than Midwest but is still profitable).

framework: Revenue drivers: number of surgeries, patient mix (payer type), invoiced price per payer, other charges (bed, medicines), post-surgery revenue
Cost drivers: Fixed costs (hospital/facilities, doctors, equipment, insurance, licenses) and Variable costs (visiting doctors/surgeons, government regulations, materials)
Customer analysis: age group, insurance coverage, payment ability
Competitive landscape: pricing, patient mix, facilities/equipment of competitors

questions.prompt: Would it be advisable to stop catering to Medicare patients (assuming no regulatory backlash)?
questions.guidance: Candidates should recognize that even though Medicare patients are unprofitable on a fully allocated cost basis, they still contribute above variable (marginal) cost. Eliminating them would reduce revenue that currently helps cover fixed costs, making the situation worse. The department may also serve as a loss leader generating synergies with other hospital departments. Recommendation: do NOT stop Medicare surgeries.

math.setup: Compare invoiced price per Medicare surgery to both fully allocated cost per surgery and variable cost per surgery.
steps: Total cost per surgery = Total Costs / # Surgeries = $21M / 1,000 = $21,000
Marginal (variable) cost per surgery = Total VC / # Surgeries = $14M / 1,000 = $14,000
math.answer: Medicare patients are unprofitable on a fully allocated basis ($15k revenue vs $21k fully loaded cost) but generate $1,000 above variable cost per surgery, helping cover $7M in fixed costs. Dropping Medicare patients is not recommended.

questions.prompt: What is the number of surgeries Midwest Hospital needs to conduct per year to break even?
questions.guidance: Candidate should calculate average revenue per surgery across the current patient mix, subtract average variable cost to get contribution margin per surgery, then divide fixed costs by that margin to find the breakeven volume. A strong answer also breaks the breakeven volume into the three patient-type buckets using the existing mix percentages.

math.setup: Breakeven = Fixed Costs / (Average Revenue per Surgery - Average Variable Cost per Surgery). Use current patient mix percentages from Exhibit 1 to decompose breakeven volume by payer.
steps: Avg. Revenue per Surgery = Total Revenue / # Surgeries = $19M / 1,000 = $19,000
Avg. Variable Cost per Surgery = Total VC / # Surgeries = $14M / 1,000 = $14,000
Breakeven Surgeries = Fixed Costs / CM per Surgery = $7M / $5,000 = 1,400 surgeries
Patient mix at breakeven (using current 10%/30%/60% split): Commercial = 10% x 1,400 = 140; Insurance = 30% x 1,400 = 420; Medicare = 60% x 1,400 = 840
math.answer: Midwest Hospital needs 1,400 surgeries per year to break even: 140 Commercial, 420 Insurance, and 840 Medicare (assuming current patient mix proportions).

questions.prompt: Why is Competitor D able to stay profitable despite having fewer commercial patients and a worse (more Medicare-heavy) patient mix than Midwest Hospital?
questions.guidance: Candidates should acknowledge that on the surface Comp D's situation looks harder than Midwest's (5% commercial, 75% Medicare vs. 10%/60%). Possible explanations: Comp D has a lower cost structure, better cost controls, or has successfully negotiated higher reimbursement rates from payers (including Medicare). This suggests Midwest should benchmark costs and explore renegotiating payer contracts.

brainstorming.prompt: What are the potential risks to increasing the number of surgeries as a strategy to reach breakeven?

categories.name: Market demand
ideas: Insufficient local market demand to support 40% volume growth
Growth may require stealing share from competitors rather than growing the overall market

categories.name: Competitive response
ideas: Competitors may retaliate with price cuts, triggering a price war
Competitor acquisition of surgeons or facilities could limit Midwest's capacity to grow

categories.name: Operational quality
ideas: Higher surgical volume may strain staff, reducing quality of care
Adverse outcomes or complications could damage the department's reputation

categories.name: Workforce
ideas: Difficulty recruiting or retaining qualified surgeons at scale

recommendation: Do not eliminate Medicare patients; they contribute above variable cost and help cover fixed costs
Increase total surgical volume toward the 1,400 breakeven threshold by marketing to more commercial and insured patients to improve mix
Renegotiate reimbursement rates with insurance and Medicare payers (benchmarking against Competitor D, which is profitable with a worse mix)
Evaluate the joint replacement department as a potential loss leader that drives patient flow and synergies across other hospital departments
risks: Insufficient demand to reach 1,400 surgeries without taking market share from competitors
Competitive retaliation if Midwest aggressively pursues commercial/insured patients
Quality or reputational risk from rapid volume growth
Failure to negotiate better reimbursement rates
next_steps: Conduct detailed cost benchmarking against Competitor D to identify cost reduction opportunities
Initiate conversations with insurance and Medicare reimbursement providers about pricing
Analyze revenue and referral synergies between joint replacement and other hospital departments
Assess post-care services (follow-up visits, physical therapy, medications) as an additional revenue stream
